pron:was.tx: From Middle High German waȥ, from Old High German waȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷod. Cognate with Dutch wat, Low German wat, English what, Danish hvad, Icelandic hvað.

det:was.tx: From Middle High German waȥ, from Old High German waȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷod. Cognate with Dutch wat, Low German wat, English what, Danish hvad, Icelandic hvað.

adv:was.tx: From Middle High German waȥ, from Old High German waȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷod. Cognate with Dutch wat, Low German wat, English what, Danish hvad, Icelandic hvað.

intj:was.tx: From Middle High German waȥ, from Old High German waȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Germanic *hwat, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷod. Cognate with Dutch wat, Low German wat, English what, Danish hvad, Icelandic hvað.

adj:warm.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German warm.

intj:wallah.tx: Borrowed from Arabic وَٱللّٰه (wal-lāh, “I swear by God”), likely via Turkish valla.

adv:wallah.tx: Borrowed from Arabic وَٱللّٰه (wal-lāh, “I swear by God”), likely via Turkish valla.

pron:wir.tx: From Middle High German wir, from Old High German wir, from Proto-West Germanic *wiʀ, from Proto-Germanic *wīz, from Proto-Indo-European *wéy. Compare Low German wi, Dutch wij, English we, Danish vi, Icelandic vér, Gothic 𐍅𐌴𐌹𐍃 (weis).

noun:Wissenschaft.tx: From late Middle High German wissenschaft (“certificate”); by surface analysis, Wissen (“knowledge”) + -schaft (“-ship; making”). Akin to Alemannic German Wüsseschaft, Bavarian Wissnschoft, Dutch wetenschap, Low German Wetenschop, West Frisian wittenskip, Danish videnskab, Norwegian Bokmål vitenskap and Swedish vetenskap.

noun:Wörterbuch.tx: From Wort (“word”) + -er- + Buch (“book”). Cognate with English wordbook, Dutch woordenboek, West Frisian wurdboek, Danish ordbog, Faroese orðabók, Icelandic orðabók, Norwegian Bokmål ordbok, Norwegian Nynorsk ordbok, Swedish ordbok and Volapük vödabuk.

noun:Welt.tx: Inherited from Middle High German wëlt, assimilative contraction of older wërlt, from Old High German wëralt, from Proto-West Germanic *weraldi, from Proto-Germanic *weraldiz. Cognate to English world, Dutch wereld, Swedish värld.

noun:Wermut.tx: From Middle High German wërmuote, from Old High German werimuota, from Proto-West Germanic *warjamōdā.

noun:Witz.tx: From Middle High German witz, from Old High German wizzi, from Proto-West Germanic *witi, from Proto-Germanic *witją from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“see, know”). Cognate to English wit, archaic Dutch wit, akin to Old Saxon giwit.

verb:wiegen.tx: From Middle High German wigen, a north-western variant of wëgen, from generalisation of the latter's present singular forms (wige, wiges, wiget). Further from Old High German wëgan, from Proto-West Germanic *wegan. Cognate with Luxembourgish weien, Dutch wegen, English weigh, Danish veje, Icelandic vega. The original ë-form is preserved in the doublet wägen, which is now chiefly restricted to …

verb:wägen.tx: From Middle High German wëgen, from Old High German wëgan. Doublet of wiegen. Compare Dutch wegen, English weigh, Danish veje, Swedish väga.

noun:Waffe.tx: From Middle High German wāfen, from Old High German wāfan (compare Yiddish וואָפֿן (vofn)), from Proto-West Germanic *wāpn, from Proto-Germanic *wēpną. Cognate with Dutch wapen, English weapon, Danish våben, Swedish vapen, Gothic 𐍅𐌴𐍀𐌽 (wēpn). Doublet of Wappen (“coat of arms”), which is borrowed from Low German.

noun:Weltschmerz.tx: Coined by German writer Jean Paul, from Welt + Schmerz.

adv:weg.tx: Shortened from Middle High German enwec, from Old High German in weg, corresponding to modern in + Weg. The first syllable is still seen in dialectal forms with e-; compare Luxembourgish ewech. Cognate with Dutch weg, Hunsrik wech, English away.

conj:weg.tx: Shortened from Middle High German enwec, from Old High German in weg, corresponding to modern in + Weg. The first syllable is still seen in dialectal forms with e-; compare Luxembourgish ewech. Cognate with Dutch weg, Hunsrik wech, English away.

adj:weg.tx: Shortened from Middle High German enwec, from Old High German in weg, corresponding to modern in + Weg. The first syllable is still seen in dialectal forms with e-; compare Luxembourgish ewech. Cognate with Dutch weg, Hunsrik wech, English away.

adv:wie.tx: From Middle High German wie, a merger of two interrelated forms: 1.) Old High German hwio, from older hwēo, from Proto-Germanic *hwaiwa; cognate with Gothic 𐍈𐌰𐌹𐍅𐌰 (ƕaiwa). 2.) Old High German hwē, hwie, from Proto-Germanic *hwē; cognate with Gothic 𐍈𐌴 (ƕē). The latter is a variant of Proto-Germanic *hwī, whence English why, and is further a fossilized instrumental case of *hwaz, *hwat (“who, …

conj:wie.tx: From Middle High German wie, a merger of two interrelated forms: 1.) Old High German hwio, from older hwēo, from Proto-Germanic *hwaiwa; cognate with Gothic 𐍈𐌰𐌹𐍅𐌰 (ƕaiwa). 2.) Old High German hwē, hwie, from Proto-Germanic *hwē; cognate with Gothic 𐍈𐌴 (ƕē). The latter is a variant of Proto-Germanic *hwī, whence English why, and is further a fossilized instrumental case of *hwaz, *hwat (“who, …

noun:Wasser.tx: From Middle High German waȥȥer, from Old High German waȥȥar, from Proto-West Germanic *watar, from Proto-Germanic *watōr, from Proto-Indo-European *wédōr, collective of *wódr̥. Compare Low German Water, Dutch water, English water, Danish vand.

adj:wichtig.tx: From the same root as Gewicht (“weight”) + -ig (“-y”), thus pertaining to wiegen (“to weigh”). See also gewichtig, a (formal or elevated) synonym of wichtig. Weight is often used as a metaphor for importance; compare German schwerwiegend (“serious, grave”), as well as English weighty, heavy.

noun:Wasserstoff.tx: From Wasser (“water”) + Stoff (“substance”), calque of French hydrogène which is itself a compound modelled after Ancient Greek ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + γεννάω (gennáō, “I bring forth”). Compare Dutch waterstof and Polish wodór.

noun:Wein.tx: From Middle High German wīn, from Old High German wīn, from Proto-West Germanic *wīn.

adj:wert.tx: From Middle High German wert, from Old High German werd, from Proto-Germanic *werþaz. See the English cognate worth for more.

adj:wild.tx: Inherited from Middle High German wilde, from Old High German wildi, from Proto-West Germanic *wilþī, from Proto-Germanic *wilþijaz.

adj:willkommen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German willekomen, from Old High German willechomen, from Proto-Germanic *wiljakumô. Cognate to Dutch welkom, English welcome, Danish velkommen, and other Germanic forms. Cognate with Portuguese bem-vindo, French bienvenu, Italian benvenuto, Spanish bienvenido, possibly Germanic calques.

intj:willkommen.tx: Inherited from Middle High German willekomen, from Old High German willechomen, from Proto-Germanic *wiljakumô. Cognate to Dutch welkom, English welcome, Danish velkommen, and other Germanic forms. Cognate with Portuguese bem-vindo, French bienvenu, Italian benvenuto, Spanish bienvenido, possibly Germanic calques.

adj:wesentlich.tx: From Middle High German wësenlīch, a calque of Latin essentialis. By surface analysis, Wesen + -t- + -lich.

verb:werken.tx: From Middle High German wërken, from Old High German werkōn, werhōn, from Proto-Germanic *werkōną. Cognate with Old Saxon werkōn, Old Dutch wirkon.

noun:Wildschwein.tx: Inherited from Middle High German wiltswīn. By surface analysis, wild + Schwein.

noun:Welle.tx: From Middle High German welle, from Old High German wella, from Proto-West Germanic *wallijā, from Proto-Germanic *wallijǭ (“wave, swirl”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn, coil”). Cognate to Old English wealca (“billow”), Albanian valë (“wave”).

noun:Windschatten.tx: Wind + Schatten, literally “shadow of the wind”.

adj:weiblich.tx: From Middle High German wīplich, from Old High German wīblīh, from Proto-Germanic *wībalīkaz, equivalent to Weib + -lich. Cognate with Dutch wijfelijk, English wifely.

noun:Weisheit.tx: From Middle High German wīsheit, from Old High German wīsheit. By surface analysis, weis + -heit.

verb:weinen.tx: From Middle High German weinen, from Old High German weinōn (“to cry, lament, cry woe”), from Proto-Germanic *wainōną (“to cry, weep”), from Proto-Indo-European *wáy (“woe”). Related with Weh, English woe, which see. Cognate with Dutch wenen (“to weep, to cry”), Old English wānian (“to complain, lament”).

pron:wer.tx: From Middle High German wër, from Old High German wër, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaʀ. Related to wo.

adv:wo.tx: With a widespread dialectal shift from -ā- to -ō-, from Middle High German wā, wār, from Old High German wār, hwār, from Proto-West Germanic *hwār, from Proto-Germanic *hwēr, *hwar. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís, whence also wer. Cognate with English where.

conj:wo.tx: With a widespread dialectal shift from -ā- to -ō-, from Middle High German wā, wār, from Old High German wār, hwār, from Proto-West Germanic *hwār, from Proto-Germanic *hwēr, *hwar. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís, whence also wer. Cognate with English where.

pron:wo.tx: From Old High German hwār, the now-extinct dative case of was. Used today in all cases.

adv:wann.tx: From Middle High German wanne, Old High German wanne, from Proto-West Germanic *hwannā, *hwan, from Proto-Germanic *hwan. Cognate with English when.

conj:wann.tx: From Middle High German wanne, Old High German wanne, from Proto-West Germanic *hwannā, *hwan, from Proto-Germanic *hwan. Cognate with English when.

noun:Wurm.tx: From Middle High German wurm, from Old High German wurm, from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis. Cognate with Dutch worm, English worm, West Frisian wjirm, Danish orm, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌼𐍃 (waurms).

noun:Wald.tx: From Middle High German walt, from Old High German wald, from Proto-West Germanic *walþu. Cognates Cognate with Dutch woud, Old English weald (English weald, wold), Old Norse vǫllr (Faroese vøllur, Norwegian Bokmål voll, Norwegian Nynorsk voll, Icelandic völlur).

noun:Wurzel.tx: From Middle High German wurzel, from Old High German wurzala, from Proto-Germanic *wurt- + *waluz. Compare Dutch wortel, Luxembourgish Wuerzel, Hunsrik Worzel, Low German Wuddel, Wortel, Vilamovian wücuł, West Frisian woartel, Old English wyrtwalu, Middle English wortwale; cf. modern English wort.

adj:weiß.tx: From Middle High German wīȥ, from Old High German wīȥ, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīt, from Proto-Germanic *hwītaz, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱweytos (“bright; shine”).

adv:warum.tx: From Middle High German warumme, war umme, warumbe, war umbe, from Old High German wār umbe. Equivalent to wo (“where”) + um (“in order to, for the purpose of”), thus “for what purpose”. Doublet of worum, but with the older vocalism preserved. Compare Dutch waarom, which has both meanings.

verb:widersprechen.tx: From Middle High German widersprëchen, from Old High German widarsprëchan, widarsprëhhan, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþrasprekan, equivalent to wider- + sprechen. Related to English withspeak.

prep:wider.tx: From Middle High German wider, from Old High German widar, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþr, from Proto-Germanic *wiþrą (“against, toward”). The same word as wieder (“again”) with artificial orthographic distinction. Hence cognate with Dutch weer, English wither.

noun:Waffenstillstand.tx: From Waffen (“weapon”) + Stillstand (“standstill”), a calque of French armistice. Compare Dutch wapenstilstand.

noun:Wade.tx: From Middle High German wade, from Old High German wado, from Proto-Germanic *waþwô (“curve; muscle; calf of the leg”), from Proto-Indo-European *wat- (“curved”).

noun:Wal.tx: The root descends from Middle High German wal, from Old High German wal, from Proto-West Germanic *hwal, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷálos (“sheatfish”). Cognates include English whale, German Low German Waal, Icelandic hvalur, Danish hval, Swedish val. Although the simplex root also existed in earlier historical stages of German, Grimm claims that the simplex had …

noun:Walker.tx: From Middle High German walker, welker, from Old High German walkāri, from Proto-West Germanic *walkārī; equivalent to walken (“to full, to walk wool”) + -er.

noun:Wall.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German wal, from Proto-West Germanic *wall, from Latin vallum. Cognate with English wall.

noun:Wand.tx: From Middle High German want, from Old High German want, from Proto-Germanic *wanduz (“fence, wall”), from Proto-Indo-European *wendʰ- (“to turn; bend; wind; twist; braid; weave”). Cognate with English wand although developing a completely distinct meaning.

noun:Ware.tx: From Middle Low German ware, from Old Saxon war (“true”).

noun:Watt.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German wat, from Proto-Germanic *wadą.

noun:Weber.tx: From Middle High German webære, from Old High German weberi, equivalent to weben (“to weave”) + -er. Cognate with Luxembourgish Wiewer, English weaver.

noun:Weg.tx: From Middle High German wëc, from Old High German wëg, from Proto-West Germanic *weg. Cognate with Dutch weg, Afrikaans weg, English way.

noun:Weltanschauung.tx: From Welt (“world”) + Anschauung (“outlook, view”), first attested in Immanuel Kant's Kritik der Urteilskraft (Critique of Judgment, 1790).

noun:Wert.tx: From Middle High German wert, from Old High German werd, from Proto-Germanic *werþaz. The -t is generalised from the uninflected form, likely reinforced by the desire to distinguish from forms of werden (compare werten). The regular -d- remains in Würde, würdig. Compare Dutch waard, English worth, Swedish värd.

noun:West.tx: From Middle High German west, from Old High German *west, from Proto-West Germanic *westr. Compare Dutch west, English west, West Frisian west, Danish vest.

noun:Whisky.tx: Borrowed from English whisky, from Scottish Gaelic uisge-beatha (literally “water of life”).

noun:Wiener.tx: From Wien + -er. (sausage): Gender from Wiener Wurst f

noun:Wild.tx: From Middle High German wilt, from Old High German wild, from Proto-Germanic *wilþaz (z-stem), from the root of *wilþijaz (“wild”). Cognate with Dutch wild, Old English wildor.

noun:Wind.tx: From Middle High German wint, from Old High German wint, from Proto-West Germanic *wind. Compare Dutch wind, English wind, Danish vind, Gothic 𐍅𐌹𐌽𐌳𐍃 (winds).

noun:Winkel.tx: From Middle High German winkel, from Old High German winkil, from Proto-West Germanic *winkil (“angle, corner”), from Proto-Indo-European *weng- (“to bend, bow, arch, curve”). Cognate with Dutch winkel, Old English wincel.

noun:Winker.tx: From Middle High German winker, winkære, equivalent to winken (“to wave”) + -er.

noun:Winter.tx: From Middle High German winder, winter, from Old High German wintar, from Proto-West Germanic *wintru, from Proto-Germanic *wintruz. Compare Dutch winter, English winter, Danish vinter.

noun:Wisent.tx: Partly inherited from, and partly a 19th-century revival of, Middle High German wisent (Brehms Tierleben, 1863–1869), from Old High German wisunt, wisant, from Proto-Germanic *wisundaz. Due to the learned origin, typically pronounced with a full vowel in the unstressed syllable. Doublet of Bison.

noun:Wolf.tx: From Middle High German wolf, from Old High German wolf, from Proto-West Germanic *wulf, from Proto-Germanic *wulfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos. Compare Dutch and English wolf, Danish ulv, Gothic 𐍅𐌿𐌻𐍆𐍃 (wulfs).

noun:Wort.tx: From Middle High German wort. Compare Dutch woord, English word, Danish ord. Doublet of Verb.

noun:Wrack.tx: From Middle Low German wrak, probably from Old Saxon *wrak, derived from wrekan, from Proto-West Germanic *wrekan, from Proto-Germanic *wrekaną, whence also German rächen and English wreak. Cognate with Dutch wrak, English wrack, wreck, Norwegian Bokmål vrak, Norwegian Nynorsk vrak, Swedish vrak (from Low German).

adv:wieder.tx: From Middle High German wider, whence English widdershins via Middle Low German borrowing; from Old High German widar, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþr (“toward, against”). Cognate with English wither.

noun:Wabe.tx: From Middle High German wabe, from Old High German waba f, wabo m, from the root of weben (“to weave”). Originally restricted to Upper German, standardized around 1800. A Central German synonym was Roß (Middle High German rāz), compare Dutch raat.

intj:wayne.tx: From English Wayne, which sounds somewhat similar to German wen (“whom”, pronounced [veːn] or [ʋeːn]). The sense is derived from trick questions of the sort: „Kennst du Wayne?“ – ? – „Wayne interessiert’s.“, that is: wen interessiert's. (“Do you know Wayne?” – ? – “Wayne cares.” [= “Who cares.”]).

noun:Warze.tx: From Middle High German warze, Old High German warza, from Proto-Germanic *wartǭ. Cognate with Old Norse varta, Old English wearte, Dutch wrat (“to grow”), English wart, Gothic *𐍅𐌰𐍂𐍄𐍉 (*wartō).

noun:Wolfram.tx: Uncertain. Compare Wulf (“wolf”) and Middle High German ram (“dirty mark, soot”).

noun:Wurst.tx: From Middle High German wurst, from Old High German wurst, from Proto-West Germanic *wursti.

verb:wehren.tx: From Middle High German weren, from Old High German werien, from Proto-West Germanic *warjan, from Proto-Germanic *warjaną.

noun:Wehr.tx: From Middle High German were, from Old High German werī, from Proto-Germanic *warīniz, derived from *warjaną, whence German wehren. Cognate with Dutch weer, Swedish värn and Danish værn, but not with English war (see there for more).

noun:Wessi.tx: Derived from Westen (“west”) + -i, analogically to Ossi, which compare for more.

noun:Wecken.tx: From Middle High German wecke, from Old High German wecki, weggi (“wedge; wedge-shaped baked good”), from Proto-Germanic *wagjaz (“wedge”). Cognate with Dutch wig (“wedge”), English wedge; also Lithuanian vãgis (“hook, peg”).

noun:Wanze.tx: From Middle High German wanze, formed with the contractive suffix -ze (cf. Spatz, Heinz) from older Middle and Old High German wantlūs (“bug”, literally “wall louse”), equivalent to Wand + Laus.

verb:werden.tx: From Middle High German wërden, from Old High German wërdan, from Proto-West Germanic *werþan, from Proto-Germanic *werþaną. Cognate with Dutch worden, obsolete English worth, Swedish varda, Norwegian Nynorsk verta, and also with Latin vertō (“to turn”). The use as a passive auxiliary is old and found throughout West Germanic, but the use as a future auxiliary is a Middle High German innovation. …

pron:welche.tx: From Middle High German welch, wilich, from Old High German welih, wilih, from Proto-Germanic *hwilīkaz.

verb:wandern.tx: From Middle High German wandern, from Old High German *wantarōn, from Proto-West Germanic *wandarōn.

verb:wohnen.tx: From Middle High German wonen, from Old High German wonēn, from Proto-West Germanic *wunēn, from Proto-Germanic *wunāną, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”). Cognate with Bavarian wohna, Alemannic German wohne, Hunsrik wohne.

verb:wissen.tx: From Middle High German wiȥȥen and Old High German wiȥȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *witan, from Proto-Germanic *witaną, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyde (“to see, to know”). Compare Dutch weten, Danish vide, Swedish veta, English wit and Latin videō (“to see”).

noun:Waage.tx: From Middle High German wāge, from Old High German wāga, from Proto-West Germanic *wāgu (“scales”). Cognate with Dutch waag, English wey. The spelling Waage was used alongside Wage since at least the 17th century. As the etymological school of the 19th century favoured single vowels, some doubled spellings like baar, Schooß, Waage were abolished during the reforms of the early 20th century. …

noun:Wiege.tx: From Middle High German wige (“cradle”), from Old High German wīga, wiega, referring to movement and therefore likely related to Proto-West Germanic *waggjan (“to cause to move”).

noun:Wurf.tx: From Middle High German wurf, from Old High German wurf, from Proto-Germanic *wurpiz, from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (“to turn, bend, twist”). Deverbal from werfen.

verb:werfen.tx: From Middle High German wërfen, from Old High German wërfan, from Proto-West Germanic *werpan, from Proto-Germanic *werpaną. Cognate with Old Saxon werpan, Dutch werpen, English warp.

noun:Wimper.tx: From Middle High German winbrā, wintprā, variants of Middle High German wintbrā, wintbrāwe, from Old High German wintbrāwa, from wint + brāwa; see Braue for the second component. It has been theorised that the first component may be cognate with Old Prussian wanso (“first hairs on the face”) and thence with Russian усы (usy, “moustache”), as well as Ancient Greek ἴονθος (íonthos, “downy hair”) …

noun:WLAN.tx: Borrowed from English WLAN, an initialism of wireless local area network.

adv:wurst.tx: According to Duden, it is derived from the noun Wurst (“sausage”), but the connection is unclear.

conj:wenn.tx: From Middle High German wanne, wenne, from Old High German hwanne, hwenne, from Proto-West Germanic *hwan, similar to the adverb wann.

verb:waschen.tx: From Middle High German waschen, from Old High German wascan, waskan, from Proto-West Germanic *waskan. Cognate with Low German waschen, Dutch wassen, English wash, West Frisian waskje, Danish vaske.

noun:Walnuss.tx: 17th century, from Low German, from Middle Low German walnut, from Proto-West Germanic *walhahnut, from Proto-Germanic *walhaz (“foreign”) + *hnuts (“nut”). Cognate with Dutch walnoot, English walnut, and (from Middle Low German) Danish valnød etc. Equivalent to wal- (related with welsch) + Nuss; compare Middle High German welhisch nuz (alongside boumnuz). Possibly a calque of Latin nux gallica …

det:welcher.tx: From Middle High German welich, from Old High German welih, wilih, from Proto-Germanic *hwilīkaz. Compare English which.

pron:welcher.tx: From Middle High German welich, from Old High German welih, wilih, from Proto-Germanic *hwilīkaz. Compare English which.

verb:winken.tx: From Middle High German winken, from Old High German winken, from Proto-West Germanic *winkijan, alternative form of *winkōn.

noun:Walze.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German walza.

noun:Wüste.tx: From Middle High German wüeste, from Old High German wuostī, from Proto-West Germanic *wōstį̄. Equivalent to wüst + -e. Also merged with Middle High German wüestene, from Old High German wuostin, *wuostinna, from Proto-West Germanic *wōstini (through regular reduction of feminines in -en(e) to -e, compare Küche etc.). The latter is cognate with Dutch woestijn.

adj:wüst.tx: From Middle High German wüeste, from Old High German wuosti (“waste”), from Proto-West Germanic *wōstī (“desolate, waste”).

verb:wühlen.tx: From Middle High German wüelen, from Old High German wuolen, from Proto-Germanic *wōlijaną, possibly related to *wallaną (“to well up”). Cognate with Luxembourgish wullen, Vilamovian wiła, Dutch woelen, Saterland Frisian wöile.

adv:wohl.tx: From Middle High German wol, wole, from Old High German wola (“well”), from Proto-Germanic *wela, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-. Compare Dutch wel, English well, Danish vel, Swedish väl.

noun:Weizen.tx: From Middle High German weize, weizze, weitze, from Old High German weizi, weizzi. The originally predominant High German form was Weiße(n) (perhaps still in Weißbier; see there). The form with [ts] was a chiefly southern variant, which was standardised probably to avoid the homophony with the adjective weiß. Cognate with Luxembourgish Weess, Hunsrik Weize, Dutch weit, Low German Weten, West …

verb:würgen.tx: From Middle High German würgen, from Old High German wurgen, from Proto-Germanic *wurgijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *werǵʰ- (“bind, squeeze”). Cognate with Dutch wurgen, worgen, English worry.

noun:Wange.tx: From Middle High German wange, from Old High German wanga. Cognate with Dutch wang, Middle English wonges. See the latter for more.

noun:Wolle.tx: From Middle High German wolle, from Old High German wolla, from Proto-West Germanic *wullu.

noun:Walfisch.tx: From Middle High German Middle High German walfisch, Middle High German walvisch, from Old High German Old High German walfisk, Old High German walfisc. By surface analysis, Wal (“whale”) + Fisch (“fish”). Cognates include German Low German Waalfisk, Dutch walvis, West Frisian walfisk, Saterland Frisian Waalfisk.

noun:Wunde.tx: From Middle High German wunde, from Old High German wunta, from Proto-Germanic *wundō (“a wound”), from *wundaz (“wounded”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wen-. Compare Low German Wunn, Dutch wond, English wound, Icelandic und.

noun:Wagen.tx: From Middle High German wagen, from Old High German wagan, from Proto-West Germanic *wagn. Cognate with Bavarian Wågn, Dutch wagen, English wain (and wagon, borrowed from Dutch), West Frisian wein, Danish vogn, Swedish vagn. Doublet of Waggon, which was borrowed from English.

conj:weil.tx: From the accusative of Middle High German wīle (modern Weile), from Old High German wīla, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīlu, from Proto-Germanic *hwīlō.

adj:wund.tx: From Middle High German wunt, from Old High German wunt, from Proto-West Germanic *wund, from Proto-Germanic *wundaz (“wounded”), from the verb *wundōną.

noun:Wandlung.tx: From Middle High German wandelunge, wandalunge, from Old High German wantalunga (“change, exchange, trade”), from Proto-West Germanic *wandalungu, from Proto-West Germanic *wandalōn, equivalent to wandeln + -ung.

prep:willen.tx: Reflecting the oblique form of Wille due to the preposition um.

adj:wollen.tx: From Middle High German wullīn, wüllīn, from Old High German wullīn, from Proto-Germanic *wullīnaz (“woolen”), equivalent to Wolle + -en.

verb:wollen.tx: From Middle High German wollen, wöllen, wullen, wellen, from Old High German wollen, wellen, from a blend of Proto-West Germanic *willjan and *walljan, from Proto-Germanic *wiljaną and *waljaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-. Compare Low German willen, Dutch willen, English will, West Frisian wolle, Danish ville, Swedish vilja. See also wählen.

verb:warten.tx: From Middle High German warten, from Old High German wartēn, from Proto-West Germanic *wardēn, from Proto-Germanic *wardāną. Cognate with Old Saxon wardōn, Swedish vårda, English ward.

prep:wegen.tx: Shortened version of von + [genitive object] + wegen, from Middle High German von + [genitive object] + wegen, with wegen being the dative plural of wec, modern-day Weg, but with a meaning similar to Ort, Stelle, Seite.

verb:wagen.tx: From Middle High German wāgen, ultimately from Old High German wāga (“scales, balance; weight”) (see Waage), in the sense of putting something on the scales, not knowing where the balance will fall.

adv:wa.tx: Clipping of nicht wahr? (“(is it) not true?”).

verb:wringen.tx: Borrowed from German Low German wringen, from Middle Low German wringen, from Old Saxon wringan, from Proto-West Germanic *wringan, from Proto-Germanic *wringaną. German cognates include ringen, renken and würgen. Compare also Low German wringen, Dutch wringen, English wring.

verb:waten.tx: From Middle High German waten, from Old High German watan, from Proto-Germanic *wadaną. The form is East Central German with open-syllable lengthening before -t-; compare the variants above.

adj:weit.tx: From Middle High German wīt, from Old High German wīt, from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz. Compare Low German wied, Hunsrik weid, Dutch wijd, English wide, Danish vid.

adv:weit.tx: From Middle High German wīt, from Old High German wīt, from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz. Compare Low German wied, Hunsrik weid, Dutch wijd, English wide, Danish vid.

noun:Wut.tx: From Middle High German wuot, from Old High German wuot, from Proto-West Germanic *wōd, from Proto-Germanic *wōdaz. Cognate with Icelandic Óðinn, English wode, English Wednesday, etc.

noun:Wetter.tx: From Middle High German wëter, from Old High German wëtar, from Proto-Germanic *wedrą, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁dʰrom, from *h₂weh₁- (“to blow; wind”) + *-dʰrom (instrument noun–deriving suffix). Compare Alemannic German Wätter, German Low German Weder, Luxembourgish Wieder, Dutch weer, English weather, Danish vejr.

noun:Witwe.tx: From Middle High German witewe, from Old High German wituwa, from Proto-West Germanic *widuwā, from Proto-Germanic *widuwǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂ (“widow”). Germanic cognates include Dutch weduwe, Old Saxon widowa, Old English widuwe, whence English widow, which see.

noun:Wette.tx: From Middle High German wette, from Old High German wetti, from Proto-West Germanic *wadi. Compare English wage.

verb:wetten.tx: From Middle High German wetten, from Old High German wettōn, from Proto-West Germanic *waddjōn, from Proto-Germanic *wadjōną. Cognate with Dutch wedden, English wed, Danish vædde, Icelandic veðja, Yiddish וועטן (vetn).

noun:Woche.tx: From Middle High German woche, from Old High German wohha, alteration of older wëhha, from Proto-West Germanic *wikā, from Proto-Germanic *wikǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *weyg- (“to bend, wind, turn, yield”). Compare Yiddish וואָך (vokh), English week, Dutch week, West Frisian wike, Danish uge, Swedish vecka.

noun:Warte.tx: From Middle High German warte, from Old High German warta, from Proto-West Germanic *wardu, from Proto-Germanic *wardō.

conj:weder.tx: From Old High German wedar, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaþar, from Proto-Germanic *hwaþeraz; cognate with English whether and either.

noun:Weltall.tx: Welt (“world”) + All (“cosmos”). Compare archaic Dutch wereldal.

verb:weisen.tx: From Middle High German wīsen, from Old High German wīsen, from Proto-West Germanic *wīsijan, from Proto-Germanic *wīsijaną.

noun:Widder.tx: From Middle High German wider, from Old High German widar, from Proto-West Germanic *weþru, from Proto-Germanic *weþruz, akin to Old Saxon wethar, English wether. The form with a short vowel is Central German, perhaps standardised in part to avoid the homophony with wider (“against”) and wieder (“again”).

noun:Wolke.tx: From Middle High German wolken, from Old High German wolkan, from Proto-West Germanic *wolkn. Akin to Dutch wolk, English welkin, Proto-Slavic *volga, Albanian ulmej (“to wet, dampen”).

conj:während.tx: From the present participle of währen (“to last, persist”), with rebracketing of währendes [noun], währender [noun], währendem [noun] as während des [noun], während der [noun], während dem [noun].

prep:während.tx: From the present participle of währen (“to last, persist”), with rebracketing of währendes [noun], währender [noun], währendem [noun] as während des [noun], während der [noun], während dem [noun].

adj:wahr.tx: From Middle High German wār, wǣre, from Old High German wār, wāri, from Proto-West Germanic *wār, from Proto-Germanic *wēraz.

verb:wenden.tx: From Middle High German wenden, from Old High German wenten, from Proto-West Germanic *wandijan.

noun:Wacholder.tx: From Middle High German [Term?], from Old High German wechalter.

verb:walzen.tx: From Middle High German, from Old High German walzan (“to turn”), from Proto-Germanic *waltaną (“to turn”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH- (“to turn”).

noun:Weile.tx: From Middle High German wīle, from Old High German wīla, from Proto-West Germanic *hwīlu. Cognate with Danish hvile (“rest”), Norwegian Bokmål hvile (“rest”), Old Norse hvíld (“rest, pause”), Gothic 𐍈𐌴𐌹𐌻𐌰 (ƕeila, “interval, time period”), English while.

noun:Weite.tx: From Middle High German wīte, from Old High German wītī; equivalent to weit + -e (“ness”). Cognate with Hunsrik Weid.

noun:Waise.tx: From Middle High German weise, from Old High German weiso; cognate with Dutch wees.

noun:Wille.tx: From Middle High German wille, from Old High German willo, from Proto-West Germanic *willjō, from Proto-Germanic *wiljô (“desire, will”), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose, wish”).

verb:wachsen.tx: From Middle High German wahsen, from Old High German wahsan, from Proto-West Germanic *wahsan. Cognate with Low German wassen, Dutch wassen, West Frisian waakse, English wax, Danish vokse, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌷𐍃𐌾𐌰𐌽 (wahsjan).

noun:Wechsel.tx: From Middle High German wëhsel, from Old High German wehsal, from Proto-Germanic *wihslaz.

noun:Wachs.tx: From Middle High German wahs, from Old High German wahs, from Proto-Germanic *wahsą. Akin to Luxembourgish Wuess, Dutch was, English wax, Danish voks, Swedish vax.

noun:Wache.tx: From Middle High German wache, from Old High German wacha, from Proto-West Germanic *waku. Cognate with Middle Dutch and Middle Low German wāke, English wake.

noun:Wärme.tx: From Middle High German werme, from Old High German warmī; analysable as warm + -e. Cognate with Hunsrik Wäärem, Luxembourgish Wäermt.

noun:Wächter.tx: From Middle High German wahtære, wahter, wähtære, wähter, from Old High German wahtāri.

noun:Wärter.tx: From Middle High German werter, from Old High German wartari.

noun:Wäsche.tx: From Middle High German wesche, from Old High German wesca, from Proto-West Germanic *waski ~ *waskiju (not attested outside High German). Cognate with Luxembourgish Wäsch, Vilamovian weś, etc. With a different stem formation compare Dutch was, Old High German wasca. By surface analysis, waschen (“to wash”) + -e.

noun:Wacht.tx: From Middle High German wahte, from Old High German wahta, from Proto-West Germanic *wahtu, from Proto-Germanic *wahtwō.

noun:Waffel.tx: Borrowed from Middle Dutch wafel. Cognate with Dutch wafel, English waffle and English wafer, Swedish våffla, Icelandic vafla.

noun:Wachtel.tx: From Middle High German wachtel, wahtel, from Old High German wahtala, wahtila, from Proto-West Germanic *hwahtlā (“quail”). The sense “prison guard” is due to similarity with the (non-derogatory) synonyms Wache and Wächter.

noun:Wahl.tx: From Middle High German wale, from Old High German wala, from Proto-West Germanic *walu, from Proto-Germanic *walą.

noun:Wahn.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German wān, from Proto-West Germanic *wāni. Not related to Wahnsinn.

noun:Wallach.tx: From Middle Low German wallache, borrowed in Prussia/Baltics from older Russian волох (volox), from Proto-Slavic *volxъ, from Proto-Germanic *walhaz. Compare Polish wałach, which is also a borrowing from East Slavic. The Slavic word means “Romance speaker”, especially one of Romania, i.e. a Wallachian or Vlach. Wallachian herdsmen are credited with having invented a new form of castration.

adj:welsch.tx: From Middle High German welsch, wälsch (wälisch, welhisch, wälhisch, walsch), from Old High German walahisc, walahisk, walask, from Proto-West Germanic *walhisk. Cognate to Dutch Waals, English Welsh, Danish vælsk. In the sense “pertaining to Wales or the Welsh language” influenced by Middle English welische, English Welsh.

noun:Wandel.tx: From Middle High German wandel, from Old High German wandil. Synchronically a deverbal of wandeln.

noun:Wanne.tx: Inherited from Middle High German wanne, from Old High German wanna, from Latin vannus, from Proto-Italic *watnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁-.

noun:Wappen.tx: From Middle High German wāpen (“weapon; coat of arms”), from Middle Low German wâpen (“weapon; coat of arms”). Doublet of Waffe (“weapon”), the High German form. The two forms were originally synonymous, but were semantically separated in early modern German.

noun:Watte.tx: Late 17th century, from Dutch watten, from Middle French ouate, of unknown origin. Despite close semantics and phonetics, probably not from Proto-Germanic *wēdiz (“garment”).

noun:Weib.tx: From Middle High German wīp, from Old High German wīb, from Proto-West Germanic *wīb. Cognate with Dutch wijf, English wife.

noun:Weiche.tx: Deverbal from weichen (“to give way”) + -e, initially to describe passing points in river shipping before being applied to railways.

verb:weichen.tx: From Middle High German wīchen, from Old High German wīchan, from Proto-West Germanic *wīkwan, from Proto-Germanic *wīkwaną, from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to bend, curve; to divide”).

adj:weich.tx: From Middle High German weich, Old High German weih. Cognate with Hunsrik weuch, Old Norse veikr (“soft, tender”), Old Saxon wēk, Old English wāc, Dutch week, English weak.

noun:Weide.tx: From Middle High German weide, from Old High German weida, from Proto-West Germanic *waiþu, from Proto-Germanic *waiþō. Cognate to Dutch weide (“pasture”).

noun:Weihnachten.tx: From Middle High German wīhenahten (“Christmas”), from a dative plural ze den wīhen nahten (“in the holy nights”). Compare modern weihen (“to hallow”) and Nacht. The oldest form (1170) is a singular diu wīhe naht (“the Holy Night”); the somewhat later plural is used to refer to the Christmas days and nights collectively. A relation with earlier heathen festivals is not endorsed by the …

verb:weihen.tx: From Middle High German wīhen, from Old High German wīhen, from Proto-West Germanic *wīhijan (“to hallow”), from Proto-Germanic *wīhijaną (“to hallow”). Cognate with Dutch wijden.

noun:Weise.tx: From Old High German wīsa, from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz (“wise”).

noun:Wende.tx: From Middle High German wende, from Old High German wendī; see wenden. Cognate to Dutch wende.

noun:Werbung.tx: werben + -ung. Cognate with English wharving from wharve.

verb:werben.tx: From Middle High German wërben, from Old High German wërban, from Proto-West Germanic *hwerban. Cognate with Dutch werven (“to recruit”), English wharve (“to turn”) Icelandic hverfa (“to turn”), Faroese hvørva (“to disappear”).

noun:Werft.tx: From earlier Werf, from Middle Low German werf, from Old Saxon hwerf (“wharf”). The sense “shipyard” probably under influence of cognate Dutch werf. Also cognate with Old High German warb, Old English hwearf, Old Norse hvarf. Derived from Proto-Germanic *hwerbaną, whence German werben. See English wharf for more.

noun:Werk.tx: From Middle High German wërc, from Old High German wërk, from Proto-West Germanic *werk, from Proto-Germanic *werką, from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom.

noun:Wunder.tx: From Middle High German wunder, wunter, from Old High German wuntar, from Proto-Germanic *wundrą, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish for, desire, strive for, win, love”). Compare German Low German Wunder, Wunner, Dutch wonder, English wonder, Danish under.

noun:Würze.tx: From Middle High German würze (ca. 1300). The form could go back through Old High German *wurza to a possible Proto-West Germanic *wurtiju, for which speaks Old Saxon wurtia. However, Pfeifer considers it a collective use of the plural of wurz (“herb, spice”), from Proto-Germanic *wrōts, *wurtiz, merged with Middle and Old High German wirz (“beerwort”), from Proto-Germanic *wirtiz, itself an …

noun:Würfel.tx: From Middle High German würfel, from Old High German wurfil, from Proto-Germanic *wurpilaz (“a die”), akin to *werpaną, both from Proto-Indo-European *werb- (“to throw, twist, bend”).

noun:Würde.tx: From Middle High German wirde, from Old High German wirdī, ultimately related to Proto-Germanic *werþaz (“valuable”). Compare English worth.

noun:Wunsch.tx: From Middle High German wunsch, from Old High German wunsc, from Proto-Germanic *wunskō, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”). Compare Dutch wens, English wish, West Frisian winsk, Danish ønske.

noun:Wucht.tx: 17th century (standard since ca. 1800), from Low German Wucht (“weight”), byform of Wicht with assimilation of the vowel to the adjacent consonants. Further from Middle Low German wicht(e), from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz. Cognate with English weight.

noun:Wuchs.tx: Deverbal from wachsen (“to grow”), past tense wuchs, by analogy with similar ablaut formations; from the 18th century.

noun:Wucher.tx: From Middle High German wuocher, from Old High German wuohhar, from Proto-Germanic *wōkraz. Compare Dutch woeker, English oker.

noun:Wonne.tx: From Middle High German wunne, wünne, from Old High German wunna, from Proto-West Germanic *wunnju (“joy”), from Proto-Germanic *wunjō (“joy”). More at winne.

noun:Wohnung.tx: From Middle High German wonunge, from Old High German wonunga, from Proto-West Germanic *wunungu, equivalent to wohnen + -ung. Related to Dutch woning (“house, residence”), English woning (“dwelling-place”). More at woning.

noun:Wirt.tx: From Middle High German wirt, wiert, wurt, wert, from Old High German wirt (“host”), from Proto-Germanic *werduz. Cognate with English ward, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹𐍂𐌳𐌿𐍃 (wairdus), Dutch waard, Danish vært and Swedish värd. The sense “caretaker; someone responsible”, which is found in compounds, developed from the sense of “host; innkeeper” due to the latter's responsibilities for his guests. However, in many …

noun:Wirbel.tx: From Middle High German wirbel, from Old High German wirbil, from Proto-Germanic *hwirbilaz.

noun:Wipfel.tx: From Middle High German wipfel, from Old High German wiphil, derived from Old High German wiphōn, from Proto-Germanic *wippōną or *wipjaną (“to sway, move back and forth”), whence modern German wippen.

noun:Windel.tx: From Middle High German windel, from Old High German wintila. Cognate with Luxembourgish Wëndel, Hunsrik Winnel.

noun:Wiese.tx: From Middle High German wise, from Old High German wisa, from Proto-West Germanic *wisā. Doublet of Wiesn (“Oktoberfest”), from Bavarian. Cognate with Luxembourgish Wiss, Middle Dutch wese, Middle Low German wēse, and the diminutives Old Saxon wiska, Middle Low German wische. Further origin uncertain. Possibly related with Proto-Germanic *wasô, whence German Wasen, and/or with Old English wīse …

noun:Weste.tx: 17th century, from French veste. At first also Veste, though the spelling with W- has always been predominant; perhaps to distinguish it from Veste (“fortress”).

noun:Wespe.tx: From Middle High German wefse, webse, wespe, from Old High German wefsa. The forms with -sp- come from Middle Low German wespe, from Old Saxon waspa (10th century, alongside older wepsia), spreading to Middle High German in the 12th century. Some Upper German dialects retain the original consonantism to this day, e.g. Swabian Wefz, Bavarian Weps, Wepsn, Webasn, Webes. The spread of -sp- was …

noun:Wesen.tx: From Middle High German wësen, from Old High German wesan (verb).

adj:weise.tx: From Middle High German wīse, from Old High German wīsi (a variant of wīs), from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz. Cognate with Dutch wijs, English wise.

verb:wellen.tx: From Middle High German wëllen. By surface analysis, Welle + -en

verb:wählen.tx: From Middle High German weln, from welen, wellen, from Old High German wellen, from Proto-West Germanic *walljan, from Proto-Germanic *waljaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁-.

adj:wenig.tx: From Middle High German weinec, wēnec (“marginal”), from Old High German *weinag, wēnag (“miserable”), from Proto-Germanic *wainagaz. The form with -ei- is original; that with -ē- arose through conflation with the morphologically simpler Old High German wē (“woe”), akin to English woe. The diphthong -ei- later on regularly became -ē- in several dialects, which further strengthened the …

noun:Werkzeug.tx: From Middle High German wercziuc, werchziuc, (also as Middle High German wercgeziuc, werchgeziuc > German Werkgezeug); equivalent to Werk (“work”) + Zeug (“gear, equipment”).

verb:weben.tx: From Middle High German weben, from Old High German weban, from Proto-West Germanic *weban. Compare Dutch weven, English weave, Danish væve.

verb:wecken.tx: From Middle High German wecken, from Old High German wecchen, from Proto-West Germanic *wakkjan (“to wake up, to awaken”).

verb:wehen.tx: From Middle High German wæjen, from Old High German wāen, from Proto-West Germanic *wāan, from Proto-Germanic *wēaną. Cognate with Dutch waaien, Old English wāwan.

adj:weh.tx: From Middle High German wē, from Old High German wē, from Proto-West Germanic *wai. Compare Latin vae, Dutch wee, English woe, Danish ve, Swedish ve, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹 (wai).

intj:weh.tx: From Middle High German wē, from Old High German wē, from Proto-West Germanic *wai. Compare Latin vae, Dutch wee, English woe, Danish ve, Swedish ve, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌹 (wai).

verb:weigern.tx: From Middle High German weigeren, from Old High German weigarōn, from Proto-West Germanic *waigrōn (“to be stubborn”).

verb:winden.tx: From Middle High German winden, from Old High German wintan, from Proto-Germanic *windaną. Cognate with Low German and Dutch winden, English wind, Danish vinde, Swedish vinda.

verb:wischen.tx: From Middle High German wischen, from Old High German wisken, from Proto-Germanic *wiskijaną.

noun:Wagner.tx: From Middle High German wagener from Old High German waganāri, equivalent to Wagen + -er.

noun:Wohl.tx: From Middle High German wole, from Old High German wolo, welo (“weal, wealth, speed, prosperity”). More at weal.

adj:wett.tx: From Middle High German wette, ultimately from the root of Wette (“bet”).

noun:Widerstand.tx: Derived from widerstehen; equivalent to wider- + Stand.

adj:wöchentlich.tx: From Woche and -lich, with umlaut (from o to ö) and epenthesis; Middle High German wochenlich.

adv:wöchentlich.tx: From Woche and -lich, with umlaut (from o to ö) and epenthesis; Middle High German wochenlich.

noun:Wassermühle.tx: Wasser + Mühle; cognate with Hunsrik Wassermihl

adv:wieso.tx: wie (“how”) + so (“so, that”). Compare the similarly constructed English how so.

noun:Wüstenspringmaus.tx: composed of Wüste, springen, and Maus

verb:walken.tx: From Middle High German walken (originally strong class 7, but later weak), from Old High German walcan, from Proto-West Germanic *walkan, from Proto-Germanic *walkaną.

noun:Weiler.tx: From Middle High German wīler, from Old High German wīlāri, from Latin vīllāre, derived from vīlla (“estate”).

noun:Weidmann.tx: From Weide (“pasture, hunting”) + Mann (“man”). Cognate to Dutch weidman (“hunter”).

noun:Welpe.tx: From Middle High German wëlf, wëlfe, from Old High German hwëlf, from Proto-West Germanic *hwelp, from Proto-Germanic *hwelpaz. The consonantism in modern Welpe is from Middle Low German welp, from Old Saxon hwelp. Cognate to English whelp.

verb:warnen.tx: From Middle High German warnen (“to watch over, protect”), Old High German warnōn (“to deny, refuse, decline”), from Proto-West Germanic *warnōn. Cognate with Old Norse varna (“to refuse”), Old Saxon wernian (“to decline, withhold”), Old English wyrnan, English warn.

noun:Wunschdenken.tx: From Wunsch (“wish”) + Denken (“thinking”). Like English wishful thinking it seems to stem from the early 20th century, it being as yet unestablished which of the two is earlier.

verb:wedeln.tx: Either from Middle High German wadelen, wedelen, from Old High German wadalōn or from the noun Wedel.

verb:wackeln.tx: From Middle High German wacken, cognate with English waggle.

phrase:wie geht's.tx: From wie geht es dir. Literally, “how does it go?”; compare English how's it going?, French comment ça va?.

verb:wiederkäuen.tx: 15th century, from wieder- (“re-, again”) + käuen (“chew”), the latter is an otherwise obsolete variant of kauen (see there).

noun:Weiher.tx: From Middle High German wī(h)er, from earlier wīwære, from Old High German wīwāri, from Proto-West Germanic *wīwārī (“pond”), from Latin vīvārium. Doublet of Vivarium.

adj:wahrscheinlich.tx: Mid-17th century, from Dutch waarschijnlijk (1540), itself a loan translation of French vraisemblable and/or Latin verisimilis (“probable”). Analysable as wahr (“true”) + scheinen (“to seem”) + -lich (“-ly”), thus “trueseemly, trueseeming”. Cognate to German Low German wohrschynlik.

adv:wahrscheinlich.tx: Mid-17th century, from Dutch waarschijnlijk (1540), itself a loan translation of French vraisemblable and/or Latin verisimilis (“probable”). Analysable as wahr (“true”) + scheinen (“to seem”) + -lich (“-ly”), thus “trueseemly, trueseeming”. Cognate to German Low German wohrschynlik.

adj:witzig.tx: Formally from Middle High German wizzic, wizzec (“wise, sensible”), from Old High German wizzīg (“wise, sensible”), from Proto-West Germanic *witīg. The modern sense developed in the 18th century following the sense of the noun, thus by surface analysis, Witz (“wit/joke”) + -ig (“-y”). Related to English witty (English -y), through Old English wittiġ (“clever, wise”).

noun:Wolkenkuckucksheim.tx: From Wolke (“cloud”) + Kuckuck (“cuckoo”) + Heim (“home, dwelling, village”). Calque of Ancient Greek Νεφελοκοκκυγία (Nephelokokkugía), in Aristophanes.

noun:Waschbär.tx: wasch(en) (“(to) wash”) + Bär (“bear”), a calque of the old taxonomic name Ursus lotor, from its habit of washing its food.

verb:wundern.tx: From Middle High German wundern, from Old High German wuntarōn, from Proto-Germanic *wundrōną, derived from *wundrą (“miracle”) (German Wunder).

noun:Wimpernschlag.tx: From Wimper (“eyelash, lash, cilium”) + -n- + Schlag (“flap, beat, hit, blow”).

adj:wässrig.tx: From Middle High German weȥȥeric, weȥric, weȥȥric, waȥȥeric, from Old High German waȥȥarīg, from Proto-West Germanic *watarīg. Equivalent to Wasser (“water”) + -ig.

adj:wässerig.tx: From Middle High German weȥȥeric, weȥric, weȥȥric, waȥȥeric, from Old High German waȥȥarīg, from Proto-West Germanic *watarīg. Equivalent to Wasser (“water”) + -ig.

noun:Wahrheit.tx: From Middle High German wārheit, from Old High German wārheit, from Proto-West Germanic *wārahaidu. Equivalent to wahr (“true”) + -heit (“-ness”).

noun:Wolkenkratzer.tx: From Wolke (“cloud”) + -n- + Kratzer (“scraper”), a partial calque of English skyscraper.

noun:Wirtshaus.tx: From Wirt (“host”) + -s- + Haus (“house”). Compare East Central German Wia(r)tshaus (Egerländisch).

noun:Wirtschaft.tx: From Wirt + -schaft. Cognate with Dutch waardschap, Central Franconian Wirtschaff, Hunsrik Wertschaft, English wardship.

verb:wässern.tx: From Middle High German wezzeren, wezzern, akin to Middle Low German wēteren, Middle Dutch weteren.

noun:Weinberg.tx: From Middle High German wīnberc. Analysable as Wein (“wine”) + Berg (“mountain, hill”).

noun:Werwolf.tx: From Middle High German wërwolf, from Old High German wërwolf, from Proto-West Germanic *werawulf (literally “man-wolf”).

noun:Wampe.tx: Upper German variant of Wamme, which see.

noun:Weihrauch.tx: From Old High German wīhrouh (“incense”), equivalent to weih (“holy”) + Rauch (“smoke”). Cognate with Dutch wierook (“incense”).

adj:wackelig.tx: From wackeln (“to waggle, wobble”) + -ig (“-y”), 17th c.; cognate with Hunsrik wacklich.

noun:Windhund.tx: From Wind + Hund (“dog”), perhaps adapted from older wendisch (“Wendish”).

noun:Witwer.tx: From Middle High German witewære, witewer, witwer, from Old High German wituwo.

noun:Wochenende.tx: Compound of Woche (“week”) + -n- + Ende (“end”). In the older language sporadically for “end of the week”. The modern sense since the 19th century after English weekend, in general use since ca. 1920.

noun:Wachstum.tx: From Middle High German wahstuom, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wahstmaz (“growth”). By surface analysis, wachsen + -tum. Cognate with Old English wæstm (“growth, increase, produce, fruit”).

adv:weiland.tx: Inherited from Middle High German wīlent, wīlen, from Old High German wīlūn, wīlōm, ultimately from the instrumental or dative plural of Proto-West Germanic *hwīlu (whence Weile). Cognate with English whilom, Dutch wijlen.

adj:wunderbar.tx: From Middle High German wunderbære (also wunderberen, wunderberende), equivalent to Wunder + -bar. Akin to German Low German wunnerbaar, Low German wunnerbor, Dutch wonderbaar, Saterland Frisian wunderboar, and also calques Danish, Norwegian Bokmål and Swedish underbar.

adj:wunderlich.tx: From Middle High German wunderlich, wonderlich, from Old High German wuntarlīh, from Proto-West Germanic *wundralīk, from Proto-Germanic *wundralīkaz, equivalent to Wunder + -lich. Cognate with English wonderly.

noun:Wasserski.tx: From Wasser + Ski, after English water ski.

noun:Wildnis.tx: From Middle High German wiltnisse, wiltnüs, equivalent to wild + -nis. Compare Middle Low German wiltnisse.

noun:Webseite.tx: Web + Seite (“page”), calque of English web page.

noun:Winzer.tx: From Late Middle High German winzer, contraction of wīnzüre, wīnzürel, from Old High German wīnzuril, from Latin vīnitor. The forms in -l were enhanced with the Germanic suffix *-ilaz.

adj:winzig.tx: From late Middle High German winzic, an intensification of wenig (“little, few”); further origin uncertain. First attested in the 14th century.

verb:wiehern.tx: 15th century, iterative of Middle High German wihen, from Old High German wihōn. Probably related with Icelandic hvía.

verb:widerlegen.tx: From Middle High German widerlegen, from Old High German widarleggen. Equivalent to wider- + legen. Compare Dutch weerleggen, Swedish vederlägga.

noun:Wahnsinn.tx: Back-formation from wahnsinnig. Not related to Wahn.

intj:Wahnsinn.tx: Back-formation from wahnsinnig. Not related to Wahn.

noun:Wandelstern.tx: Equivalent to wandeln (“to wander, stroll about”) + Stern (“star”). Compare English wandering star, wanderstar.

verb:wichsen.tx: From Middle High German wihsen, Old High German wahsen (“to wax”).

verb:wirken.tx: From Middle High German wirken, from Old High German wirken, from Proto-West Germanic *wirkijan, from Proto-Germanic *wirkijaną. Early on merged with Middle High German würken, from Old High German wurken, from Proto-West Germanic *wurkijan, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną, closely related to the first-mentioned verb. The i-form prevailed in Central German, the ü-form in Upper German; the latter …

verb:wahrnehmen.tx: From Middle High German war nëmen, from Old High German wara nëman (literally “to take attention”).

adj:wirklich.tx: From wirk(en) + -lich. Cognate with Bavarian wirkli, wirkle, Hunsrik werklich and Dutch werkelijk.

adv:wirklich.tx: From wirk(en) + -lich. Cognate with Bavarian wirkli, wirkle, Hunsrik werklich and Dutch werkelijk.

verb:wechseln.tx: From Middle High German wëhseln, from Old High German *wëhsalōn, from Proto-Germanic *wihslōną, from Proto-Indo-European *weyk-, *weyḱ- (“to change”). Compare Dutch wisselen, Luxembourgish wiesselen, dialectal English wissle, more distantly Latin vicis, English week, German Woche.

noun:Wels.tx: From Middle High German wels, from Old High German *wals, *walis, from Proto-West Germanic *hwaliʀ, from Proto-Germanic *hwalaz, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kʷálos (“sheatfish”). Cognate with German Low German Wels (“catfish”), Dutch wels (“catfish”), Old High German walira (“whale”), German Wal (“whale”).

noun:Wirrwarr.tx: 15th-century shortening of Middle High German wirrewarren n, a reduplicative ablauting derivation (cf. Mischmasch) from werren (“to entangle, confuse”), from Old High German werran, from Proto-West Germanic *werʀan.

verb:widerstehen.tx: From Middle High German widerstān, widerstēn, widerstōn, from Old High German widarstān, widarstēn, widarstantan, equivalent to wider- + stehen. Cognate with Dutch weerstaan, English withstand.

verb:wiedersehen.tx: From Middle High German widersehen, from Old High German widarsehan, widarisehan. Equivalent to wieder- + sehen.

verb:welken.tx: From Middle High German welken, from Old High German welkēn. According to Kluge, ultimately from the root of Wolke (“cloud”).

adj:welk.tx: From Middle High German welc, from Old High German welk; see the verb welken. Cognate with Hunsrik wellich.

adj:walisisch.tx: The alternative form is from Wallis + -isch.

verb:wünschen.tx: From Middle High German wünschen, wunschen, from Old High German wunsken (“to choose, wish, desire”), from Proto-West Germanic *wunskijan (“to wish”), from Proto-Germanic *wunskijaną (“to wish”), derived from *wunskaz, *wunskō (“wish, desire”), from Proto-Indo-European *wun-, *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”). Cognate with Dutch wensen (“to wish”), English wish, Danish ønske (“to wish”), and further …

verb:wetzen.tx: From Middle High German wetzen, from Old High German wezzen, hwezzen, from Proto-West Germanic *hwattjan, from Proto-Germanic *hwatjaną (“to incite, sharpen”). Cognate with English whet.

noun:Wetzstein.tx: From Middle High German wetzstein, wetzestein, from Old High German wezzistein, from Proto-West Germanic *hwattjastain. Equivalent to wetzen + Stein.

adj:widrig.tx: From Middle High German wideric, from Old High German *widarīg, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþrīg.

noun:Wehrdienstverweigerer.tx: From Wehr (“defence, defense (i.e., military, national, selective)”) + Dienst (“service”) + Verweigerer (“refuser”).

noun:Willkür.tx: From Middle High German wil(le)kür, equivalent to Wille + Kür.

noun:Wegerich.tx: From Middle High German wegerîch, wegerich, from Old High German wegarîh (literally “path-king”). By surface analysis, Weg + -rich.

noun:Winde.tx: From Middle High German winde, from Old High German *winda (attested in wazzarwinda), derived from Proto-Germanic *windaną. Doublet of winden.

noun:Wirbeltier.tx: From Wirbel (“vertebra”) + Tier (“animal”), partial calque of Latin vertebratum.

noun:Wohnwagen.tx: From wohnen (“to live, dwell, stay”) + Wagen (“vehicle, wagon, car”).

noun:Wohlstand.tx: wohl + Stand, 18th c. Compare Dutch welstand.

noun:Wellensittich.tx: From Welle (“wave”) + Sittich (“parakeet”), a calque of translingual Melopsittacus undulatus.

phrase:wie geht es Ihnen.tx: Literally, “how is it going for you”.

verb:widmen.tx: From Middle High German widemen, from Old High German widimen (“gift, give as a gift”), from widimo (“gift”), from Proto-West Germanic *weþmō (“dowry”). Synchronically analyzed as a verbal formation from Wittum (“dowry”).

noun:Wankelmut.tx: From wankeln + Mut. Cognate to Dutch wankelmoed.

noun:Walross.tx: Via Dutch walrus from an Old Norse source (cf. Danish hvalros). Secondary motivation in German as a compound of Wal (“whale”) + Ross (“horse”).

noun:Weisheitszahn.tx: Weisheit + -s- + Zahn, literally “wisdom tooth”. Calque of Latin dēns sapientae, itself calqued from Ancient Greek σωφρονιστῆρες (sōphronistêres). See English wisdom tooth for cognates.

noun:Wiedehopf.tx: From Middle High German witehopf, from Old High German witihopfa, onomatopoeic.

noun:Wortschatz.tx: Wort (“word”) + Schatz (“treasure”). Cognate with Dutch woordenschat, Afrikaans woordeskat and Luxembourgish Wuertschatz. Attested since at least 1772 (see quote); possible calque of Dutch woordenschat.

adj:wacker.tx: From Middle High German wacker, from Old High German wackar, from Proto-West Germanic *wakr, from Proto-Germanic *wakraz. See there for cognates.

noun:Wiesel.tx: From Middle High German wisele, from Old High German wisula, wisala, from Proto-West Germanic *wisulā. Compare Low German Wessel, Wissel, Dutch wezel, English weasel, Swedish vessla.

verb:wickeln.tx: From Middle High German wickeln (“to wind, wrap around”), denominative of wickel, from Old High German wickilī (“fibres wound around the distaff”), from Proto-Germanic *wīkaną (“to bend”), from Proto-Indo-European *weg- (“to weave”). Related to modern Wickel (“anything wrapped, especially a cloth around a poultice”). The Old High German noun is a diminutive of wiohha (“bundle of fibres, wick”), …

noun:Widersacher.tx: From Middle High German widersache, from Old High German widersahho, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþrasakō. The final -r is due to influence of the suffix -er, which is often used for agent nouns.

adj:willentlich.tx: From Middle High German willentlich, willentlīche, from Old High German willontlīh. By surface analysis, Willen + lich.

adv:willentlich.tx: From Middle High German willentlich, willentlīche, from Old High German willontlīh. By surface analysis, Willen + lich.

phrase:weder Fisch noch Fleisch.tx: Literally, “neither fish nor meat”. Compare with Dutch vlees noch vis, French ni chair ni poisson, Polish ni pies, ni wydra, Russian ни рыба ни мясо (ni ryba ni mjaso), and so on. Perhaps from the context of fasting (on Fridays and during Lent), where fish was allowed, but other meats were not. Or from the notion that dishes containing neither of these ingredients are not “proper” food.

noun:Weichsel.tx: 16th century, from Middle Low German Wissel, from Proto-Slavic *Visъla. The form is probably due to analogy: as wissel(-bēre) is also the Low German form of the fruit in etymology 2 below, the river name was adapted to High German accordingly.

adv:worauf.tx: Univerbation of wo + auf. By surface analysis, wo + -r- + auf.

adv:worin.tx: Middle High German worinne and newly formed Univerbation of wo inne, innen.

adv:womit.tx: Middle High German. By surface analysis, wo (“where”) + mit (“with”). Akin to archaic English wherewith.

adv:wofür.tx: Compare Dutch waarvoor (“for what”), English wherefore, Danish hvorfor (“why”), Norwegian Bokmål hvorfor (“why”), Norwegian Nynorsk korfor, kvifor (“why”), Swedish varför (“why”).

noun:Weihe.tx: From Middle High German wīhe, from Old High German wīhī. Equivalent to weih + -e.

noun:Wehmut.tx: From Middle Low German wēmōt, perhaps a backformation from wēmōdich, whence German wehmütig. Analysable as Weh (“woe”) + Mut (“mood, emotional state”). The feminine under influence of the rhyming word Demut (“humbleness”, from Middle High German demüete) or other feminines ending with -mut (like Großmut, Schwermut). From Middle Low German also continental Scandinavian vemod. Dutch weemoed is …

noun:Waffenschmied.tx: From Waffe + -n- + Schmied. Compare English weaponsmith, Swedish vapensmed.

noun:Weißbier.tx: Now predominantly considered to be from weiß (“white”) + Bier (“beer”), since the word was formerly also sometimes used for beers made from grains other than wheat. The alternative theory derives it from Weiße(n), an old and dialectally still widespread variant of Weizen (“wheat”). The latter word would seem at least to have reinforced the restriction. Cognate with Hunsrik Weisbier.

verb:wippen.tx: From Low German and Middle Low German wippen, ultimately from or related to Proto-West Germanic *waibijan (“to move back and forth”).

noun:Wucherer.tx: From Middle High German wuocherære, from Old High German wuohharāri, derived from wuohhar, whence modern German Wucher (“usury”).

verb:wurmen.tx: From Wurm (“worm”) + -en. Formally already in Middle High German wurmen and Old High German wormōn, but with unrelated senses. Since the 15th century “to have worms, be wormridden”. The contemporary meaning since the later 18th century, seemingly popularised in part by Goethe. Evoking the idea of a nibbling worm in one’s mind or conscience, perhaps remotely based on Isaiah 66:24, Mark 9:44 …

noun:Weingarten.tx: From Middle High German wīngarte, from Old High German wīngarto. Analysable as Wein (“wine”) + Garten (“garden”).

noun:Wiederkehr.tx: From Middle High German widerkēr, widerkēre, from Old High German widarkēr, widarkēra. By surface analysis, deverbal from wiederkehren.

verb:wispern.tx: 17th century, from Low German wispern, chiefly displacing the above variant, from Middle High German and Middle Low German wispelen, ultimately of imitative origin (lautmalend). The r-form could be a late alteration, but could also be old in view of Old English hwisprian, whence English whisper.

noun:Weinbrand.tx: From Wein (“wine”) + Brand (“distillation”, literally “burning”). Alteration of Branntwein, which had taken on the broader sense “distilled alcoholic drink”.

intj:wehe.tx: Variant of weh, which see. The usual distinction between the two forms was first noted by Adelung. While the Deutsches Wörterbuch (1955) considered this distinction “untenable”, it is in fact a linguistic reality, albeit with occasional exceptions.

noun:Weh.tx: From Middle High German wēwe, from Old High German wēwo, from Proto-Germanic *waiwô.

verb:wegwerfen.tx: From weg- + werfen. Compare Dutch wegwerpen.

noun:Weisel.tx: Inherited from Middle High German wīsel (“leader”); equivalent to weisen (“to show, to indicate”) + -el.

noun:Wesfall.tx: wes (“whose”) + Fall (“case”) (wes is a short form of wessen)

noun:Weichei.tx: From weich (“soft”) + Ei (“egg”). The word “egg” may be interpreted in the literal sense comparing hartgesotten and English hard-boiled, soft-boiled. It may also be interpreted in the sense “testicle” comparing French couille molle.

adj:wunderschön.tx: Wunder (“wonder”) + schön (“beautiful”). Akin to Dutch wonderschoon.

verb:wittern.tx: From Middle High German witeren, derived from Middle High German weter.

noun:Wirsing.tx: Borrowed from Lombard verza, from Vulgar Latin *virdia (“cabbage”), from Latin viridis (“green”).

adv:wiederum.tx: From Late Middle High German widerumb (15th c.). By surface analysis, wieder (“again”) + um (“around”). Compare Middle Dutch wēderomme (13th c. as wı̊der+v̊mb, modern wederom), Middle Low German wedderümme.

noun:Waggon.tx: Early 19th century, from English waggon, from Middle Dutch waghen, from Proto-Germanic *wagnaz. Doublet of inherited Wagen. The French-like pronunciation was adopted under the influence of French wagon, itself a borrowing from English.

verb:wandeln.tx: From Middle High German wandeln, from Old High German wantalōn, from Proto-West Germanic *wandalōn.

adj:willens.tx: From the genitive of Wille (“will”), originally a genitive of quality (i.e. "having will").

verb:wälzen.tx: From Middle High German welzen, from Old High German welzen, from Proto-West Germanic *waltijan.

noun:Wegweiser.tx: Weg (“way”) + Weiser (“sage, guide”) Cognate to Danish vejviser, Swedish vägvisare, Icelandic vegvísir.

verb:wachen.tx: From Middle High German wachen, from Old High German wahhēn, from Proto-West Germanic *wakēn, from Proto-Germanic *wakāną. Cognate to English wake.

noun:Want.tx: From Middle Dutch want, gewant, from Old Dutch *giwant, from Proto-Germanic *gawandą, from the root of winden.

noun:Wollust.tx: From Old High German wolalust, willilust (“lust”), formed from wola (ancestral to modern wohl) + lust (ancestral to modern Lust).

adj:windig.tx: From Middle High German windic, equivalent to Wind + -ig. Compare English windy.

verb:weitersagen.tx: From weiter- + sagen, literally, “to say further”.

noun:Walküre.tx: 18th century, from Old Norse valkyrja (“chooser of the slain”), from valr (“the slain”) + kyrja (“chooser”), from kjósa (“to choose”). The first element is related with native German Walstatt, the latter with Kür.

verb:wanken.tx: From Middle High German wanken, from Old High German wankōn, from Proto-West Germanic *wankōn, from Proto-Germanic *wankōną.

noun:Wutbürger.tx: Wut + Bürger, Wut (“rage, fury, wrath, temper, dander, frenzy, passion”) + Bürger (“citizen, burgher”). Cognate to English wode (“furious, fury”) + burgher (“citizen”).

noun:Weltreich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German werltrīche, from Old High German weraltrīhhi; by surface analysis, Welt + Reich. Compare Middle English world-riche and Dutch wereldrijk.

verb:wärmen.tx: From Middle High German wermen, from Old High German wermen, from Proto-Germanic *warmijaną. Cognate with Hunsrik wäärme, Luxembourgish wiermen.

noun:Würzsauce.tx: * From Würze less the letter -e and Sauce.

verb:wegfliegen.tx: From the compounding of the prefix weg (“away”) and fliegen (“to fly”), from Old High German fliogan (“to fly”), from Proto-Germanic *fleuganą (“to fly”).

verb:wassern.tx: From Middle High German wazzeren, wazzern, akin to Middle Low German wāteren, Middle Dutch wateren.

adj:wahnsinnig.tx: Coined in the 15th century after the model of wahnwitzig which uses as its first part the word wahn, which came from Old High German wan "missing, empty", which came from Proto-Germanic *wanaz. Not cognate with Wahn. Cognate with English wane.

adv:wahnsinnig.tx: Coined in the 15th century after the model of wahnwitzig which uses as its first part the word wahn, which came from Old High German wan "missing, empty", which came from Proto-Germanic *wanaz. Not cognate with Wahn. Cognate with English wane.

noun:Weltmeer.tx: Compound of Welt + Meer. Compare Dutch wereldzee, Swedish världshav.

noun:Wellenleiter.tx: From Welle (“wave”) + Leiter (“conductor; lead”). Calque of English waveguide.

verb:widerspiegeln.tx: wider (“against, contra-”) + spiegeln (“to reflect”). Compare Dutch weerspiegelen.

adj:wehmütig.tx: From Middle Low German wēmōdich. Analysable as Wehmut + -ig, but Middle Low German wēmōt is perhaps a backformation from the adjective. See Wehmut for more.

noun:Weinfass.tx: Equivalent to Wein (“wine”) + Fass (“keg”); from Middle High German wīnvaz, from Old High German wīnfaz, from Proto-Germanic *wīnafatą. Cognate with Icelandic vínfat.

verb:wahren.tx: From Middle High German warn, waren, from Old High German warōn, ultimately derived from Proto-West Germanic *warōn. Related to biwarōn, from wara (“attention”). Compare German bewahren.

noun:Wichse.tx: In the sense “polish” an 18th-century back-formation from wichsen (“to polish”), from a variant of wachsen (“to wax”). The former verb then developed the sense “to wank, masturbate (of a male)” based on the back-and-forth movement. The noun sense “cum, semen” thence, but plausibly reinforced by the already existing sense of the noun.

adj:wahrhaftig.tx: From Middle High German wârhaftic, equivalent to wahrhaft + -ig.

adv:wahrhaftig.tx: From Middle High German wârhaftic, equivalent to wahrhaft + -ig.

noun:Wart.tx: From Middle High German wart, warte, from Old High German wart, warto, from Proto-West Germanic *ward, *wardō, from Proto-Germanic *wardaz, *warduz, *wardô. Related with warten and wahren. Cognate with English ward.

noun:Wiel.tx: Possibly from Middle High German *wihel, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *hwehwl, from Proto-Germanic *hwehwlą (“wheel”). In the sense “bundle of rope” through Middle Low German wêl. The sense “whirlpool” may be from Low German too, but it has also been attested in southern sources (the very first being notably from Nuremberg in the 15th century). Therefore inheritance through Old High German …

noun:Widrigkeit.tx: From Middle High German widericheit, from Old High German *widarīgheit, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþrīgahaidu.

noun:Wake.tx: 17th century, from Middle Low German wāke, from Proto-Germanic *wakwō.

verb:wirren.tx: From Middle High German wërren, from Old High German wërran, from Proto-West Germanic *werʀan (“to confuse, muddle”).

verb:wabbeln.tx: From Middle High German wabelen, merged with related Middle Low German *wabbelen. To the former compare Old Norse vafla, to the latter dialectal Dutch wobbelen, English wabble, wobble. All of these are iteratives of Proto-Germanic *wabōną, related to *webaną (“to weave”), whence Middle High German waben (“to move about”), Old English wafian (modern English wave). In the High German form, the -bb- …

verb:währen.tx: From Middle High German wëren, wërn, from Old High German wërēn, from Proto-West Germanic *weʀēn, related to Old High German wesen (“to be, exist”). More at Wesen (“being, essence, creature”).

verb:weismachen.tx: From Middle High German wīs machen. By surface analysis, weise machen, literally “to make wise”. The modern sense arose in the 16th century.

noun:Wohnungsbau.tx: From Wohnung + -s- + Bau. Compare Dutch woningbouw.

adv:wahrlich.tx: By surface analysis, wahr + -lich. Compare Dutch waarlijk.

adj:widerspenstig.tx: From Middle High German widerspene, widerspān, 15th c. Compare Modern German wider- and spannen (“to tension”).

noun:Wegfall.tx: Deverbal of wegfallen (“to fall away, disappear”).

noun:Werder.tx: From Middle High German werder, enhanced form of older wert, from Old High German warid, werid, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *wariþ m or n. The suffixed form is northern and was reinforced by Middle Low German werder. Cognate with Dutch waard, Old English waroþ.

verb:wiedergeben.tx: Inherited from Middle High German widergëben, from Old High German widargëban. By surface analysis, wieder- + geben.

verb:wappnen.tx: From Wappen, which now means only “coat of arms”, but originally also meant “weapon”. Compare bewaffnen, a native High German cognate (sans the prefix), and the dated waffnen.

verb:wehtun.tx: From weh + tun. Compare Spanish hacer daño.

noun:Wedel.tx: Inherited from Middle High German wadel / wedel, from Old High German wadal / wedil, from Proto-West Germanic *waþil (“whisk”).

noun:Wau.tx: 17th century, borrowed from Dutch wouw, from Middle Dutch woude. Cognate with English weld, French gaude. Further origin unknown.

verb:weglegen.tx: From weg- + legen. Cognate with Dutch wegleggen.

verb:wegfahren.tx: From weg- + fahren. Compare English wayfare.

verb:wursteln.tx: From Wurst (“sausage”), thus originally “to make sausages” (compare wursten), and then figuratively in the sense of “to meddle, to tamper”. In Low German areas the verb is likely to have been secondarily associated with an unrelated verb meaning “to wrestle, to struggle”, attested in Middle Low German worsteln and cognate with English wrestle and Dutch worstelen. Some senses and particularly the …

verb:weihnachten.tx: Back-formation from Weihnachten, originally coined in 1862 by the poet Theodor Storm in the poem "Knecht Ruprecht".

noun:Wust.tx: From Middle High German wuost, related to wüst.

noun:Weissager.tx: In its modern form a compound of weise + Sager (“wise-sayer”). However, this is a secondary motivation of Old High German wīzzago, which is remotely related only to the former of the two components mentioned, pertaining more closely to German Wissen (“knowledge”) and thus English wit. Already in Old High German this ancient noun began to be re-interpreted as wīssago, i.e. in the modern sense.

noun:Wimpel.tx: From Proto-Germanic *wimpilaz; compare Old English wimpel.

noun:Wiederauferstehung.tx: From wiederauferstehen (“to resurrect, resurge”) + -ung, from wieder- (“again”) + auferstehen (“to resurrect, resurge”), from auf- (“up”) + erstehen (“to arise”), from er- (prefix indicating completion) + stehen (“to stand”).

adj:wendig.tx: From Middle High German wendec, wendic (“retrogressive”), from Old High German wentīg; by surface analysis, wenden + -ig (DWDS).

noun:Wicht.tx: From Middle High German wicht, from Old High German wiht (“creature, thing”), from Proto-West Germanic *wihti (“essence, object”). Cognate with Dutch wicht, English wight, Swedish vätte, and Icelandic vættur.

noun:Wimmer.tx: From wimmen, from Medieval Latin vīndēmiō (“to harvest grapes”).

verb:weiden.tx: From Middle High German weiden, from Old High German weidōn, from a derivative of Proto-West Germanic *waiþu (“pasture, grassland”).

noun:Wichte.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German wichte, from Proto-West Germanic *wihti, from Proto-Germanic *wihtiz.

verb:wähnen.tx: From Middle High German wænen, from Old High German wānen, wānnen, from Proto-West Germanic *wānijan. Cognate with English ween (“to imagine; suppose; judge”).

verb:wimmeln.tx: From Middle High German wimelen (hapax, 13th c.), frequentative of wimmen, from Old High German wimmen (“to gush, bubble, move lively”). Cognate with Dutch wemelen, Westphalian Low German wiëmeln.

adj:wehleidig.tx: 17th century, from Upper German dialects. Weh + leidig.

noun:Woge.tx: With dialectal -ā- → -ō- from northern Middle High German wāge (“wave”), borrowed from Middle Low German wāge (“wave”). The latter form could be a mere alteration of the rare masculine Middle Low German wāch (“stormy sea”), from Old Saxon wāg (“stormy sea”), from Proto-West Germanic *wāg, from Proto-Germanic *wēgaz (which see for cognates); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *weǵʰ- (“to …

verb:wallen.tx: From Middle High German wallen, from Old High German wallan (“spin, twist, dance”), from Proto-West Germanic *wallan, from Proto-Germanic *wallaną. Cognate with English to well up.

noun:Wahlkämpfer.tx: From Wahl (“election”) + Kämpfer (“fighter”) or Wahlkampf (“election campaign”) + -er.

noun:Wisch.tx: From Middle High German wisch, from Old High German -wisc (in arswisc and ovanwisc), from Proto-Germanic *wiskaz. Cognate with English whisk.

noun:Wasserrad.tx: Wasser + Rad; cognate with Hunsrik Wasserraat

noun:Wohnheim.tx: From wohnen (“to live at, to reside”) + Heim (“home”).

noun:Weihwasser.tx: From Middle High German wīchwazzer. Analyzable as weihen (“to consecrate”) + Wasser (“water”), though the former component was probably the related Middle High German adjective wīch (“holy, consecrated”). Compare Dutch wijwater.

noun:Wamme.tx: From Middle High German wambe, from Old High German wamba, from Proto-Germanic *wambō. Cognate with English womb. Wamme shows the normal Standard German development -mb- → -mm-, whereas the variant Wampe has an Upper German consonantism. The two are now usually distinguished semantically: Wamme referring to animals, Wampe to people in colloquial use.

verb:wuchern.tx: From Middle High German wuochern, from Old High German wuohharōn, derived from wuohhar (“harvest, revenue”), whence modern German Wucher (“usury”). Compare Dutch woekeren (“to practise usury; to overgrow”).

adj:widerwärtig.tx: From Middle High German widerwertic, from Old High German widerwart, equivalent to wider (“against”) + -wärtig (adjective suffix denoting position).

adv:widerwärtig.tx: From Middle High German widerwertic, from Old High German widerwart, equivalent to wider (“against”) + -wärtig (adjective suffix denoting position).

noun:Wanst.tx: From Middle High German wanst, from Old High German wanast, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wend-tri-. Cognate with Latin venter (“belly”) and Latin vēsīca (“bladder”).

noun:Wasserkopf.tx: From Wasser (“water”) + Kopf (“head”), calque of Latin hydrocephalus.

phrase:wie Pilatus ins Credo.tx: Literally, “like Pilate [got] into the creed”. Both the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed mention, apart from Jesus himself, only two human beings: Pilate and the Virgin Mary. This may be regarded an undue honour to the former; even if his being mentioned is in a negative context.

noun:Weinstein.tx: From Middle High German wīnstein. Equivalent to Wein (“wine”) + Stein (“stone”).

noun:Waschküche.tx: From waschen (“to wash, to launder”) + Küche (“kitchen”)

verb:weilen.tx: From Middle High German wīlen, from Old High German wīlōn, from or related to Proto-West Germanic *hwīlu (“period of time, rest, while”).

noun:Wäscherei.tx: From waschen or Wäsche + -erei, apparently after Middle Low German wescherīe.

noun:Wucherung.tx: From Middle High German wuocherunge, from Old High German wuohharunga. Equivalent to wuchern + -ung.

verb:waffnen.tx: From Middle High German wāfenen, from Old High German wāfanen.

adj:wahnwitzig.tx: From wahnwitz + -ig, displacing the unsuffixed form after Early New High German times.

adj:windelweich.tx: Windel (“diaper”) + weich (“soft”); surface analysis being "as soft as a diaper", hence the range of meanings.

adj:wurmstichig.tx: From late Middle High German wurmstichic, derived from wurmstich m (“wormhole”), possibly from Middle Low German wormstēke f, m (early 14th century; compare obsolete German Wurmstiche f alongside regular Wurmstich m). Analyzable as Wurm (“worm”) + Stich (“stitch, prick”) + -ig.

adj:wuschig.tx: Northern German, related to wuscheln (“to tousle”) and wuseln (“to scurry”).

noun:Weck.tx: From Middle High German wecke, from Old High German wecki, weggi (“wedge; wedge-shaped baked good”), from Proto-West Germanic *wagi, from Proto-Germanic *wagjaz (“wedge”). Cognate with Dutch wig (“wedge”), English wedge.

noun:Wolpertinger.tx: Unknown; hypotheses include a derivation from the town of Wolterdingen or from a dialectal form of Walpurgisnacht (“Walpurgis night”).

noun:Windhauch.tx: Wind (“wind”) + Hauch (“breath from the mouth; breeze”). The sense of “vanity” is ultimately a loan translation of Hebrew הבל (hevel, “steam; breath; something vain”).

noun:Weißbrot.tx: From weiß (“white”) + Brot (“bread”). Cognate with Hunsrik Weisbrod.
