noun:Wulst.tx: From Middle High German wulst m, wulste f, from Old High German wulst m, wulsta f, from Proto-West Germanic *hwulfsti, from Proto-Germanic *hwulfstiz (“curvature, vaulting, bulge”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷelp- (“to curve”). Related to German wölben (“to curve, bend, arch”), English whelm (“to engulf”).

phrase:wer's glaubt, wird selig.tx: Based on Luther's translation of Mark 16:16

noun:Weltlichkeit.tx: From Middle High German weltlīchheit, werltlīcheit, equivalent to weltlich + -keit.

verb:widerfahren.tx: From Middle High German widervarn, from Old High German widarfaran, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþarfaran. Equivalent to wider- + fahren.

noun:Wachtmeister.tx: 15/16th c., Wacht + Meister. Compare Middle High German wachemeister.

noun:Wippe.tx: Borrowed from Low German Wippe. Compare Dutch wip.

verb:walten.tx: From Middle High German walten, from Old High German waltan, from Proto-West Germanic *waldan (“to reign”), from Proto-Germanic *waldaną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁-. The Middle High German verb was conjugated as both a strong and a weak verb, suggesting a possible merger with unrecorded Old High German *waltōn, from Proto-West Germanic *waldōn, ultimately from the same source. …

phrase:wenn schon, denn schon.tx: Literally, “if already, then already”, or more properly "if at all, then actually", from a phrase such as Wenn wir es schon machen, dann lass es uns schon auch richtig machen. (“If we do it at all, then let us actually do it right.”). Denn stands in for standard dann, a usage chiefly found in Northern Germany, but the idiom has spread throughout the language area. Küpper dates it to the 19th …

noun:Wahrung.tx: Inherited from Middle High German warunge. Compare Polish warunek.

noun:Wams.tx: From Middle High German wambes, wambeis, from Old French wambais, from Medieval Latin wambāsium, bambāsium. This is predominantly considered a derivative of Frankish *wamba, from Proto-Germanic *wambō (“belly, womb”), making Wams a doublet of Wamme (“dewlap”) and Wampe (“potbelly, paunch”). Alternative etymology derives it from Latin bambax (“coton”), from Ancient Greek πάμβαξ (pámbax), in which …

noun:Walstatt.tx: From Middle High German walstat, from wal (“battlefield”, originally probably “battle, carnage”) + stat (“place”, whence modern Stadt, Statt, and Stätte). The first element is from Old High German wal, from Proto-Germanic *walaz.

noun:Wespennest.tx: From Middle High German wefsennest, from Old High German wefsunnest. Equivalent to Wespe (“wasp”) + -n- + Nest (“nest”).

phrase:wie ist es.tx: Literally, “how is it?” (compare Dutch hoe is het).

noun:Wüstenei.tx: From Middle High German wüestenīe, from Old High German wuostin. Analyzable as wüst + -ei.

noun:Werber.tx: From Middle High German wërbære, equivalent to werben + -er.

phrase:wer nie sein Brot im Bette aß, we.tx: Literally, “he who never ate his bread in bed, knows not how crumbs can prick”. Humorous alteration of a passage in Goethe's “Wilhelm Meister”: Wer nie sein Brot mit Tränen aß, / wer nie die kummervollen Nächte / auf seinem Bette weinend saß, / der kennt euch nicht, ihr himmlischen Mächte. (“He who never ate his bread with tears, / who never in sorrowful nights / sat on his bed weeping, / he …

noun:Wachtelkönig.tx: From Wachtel + König. From the 16th Century, the plumage of the bird resembles that of a quail.

noun:Werst.tx: 16th century, from Russian верста́ (verstá). The endingless form (instead of *Wersta or *Werste) is influenced by the Russian genitive plural вёрст (vjorst), which is often used after numerals.

noun:Wechselbalg.tx: wechseln (“to exchange”) + Balg (“baby, brat”). Cognate to Dutch wisselbalg.

noun:Warft.tx: Borrowed from Low German Warf, from Middle Low German warf, werf, from Old Saxon hwerf, probably from hwervan (“to turn around”). The word was first adopted as Werft (17th c.), which became specialized to the sense “shipyard” in High German. Since the 19th century, newer Low German Warf was introduced for differentiation, taking on the same unetymological -t as its doublet. Cognate with Dutch …

noun:Wegelagerer.tx: From wegelagern (“to waylay”) + -er, displacing older wegelāger. See the verb for the further development.

noun:Westwind.tx: West + Wind. Cognate with Old English westwind.

noun:Werg.tx: From Middle High German werc, wer(i)ch, from Old High German werk, werah, from Proto-West Germanic *werk, from Proto-Germanic *werką (“rope”). For the Middle High German variation between -rc and -rch compare Storch. The spelling with -g is an attempt to reflect both pronunciations; compare Sarg (from Middle High German sarc, sar(i)ch). Moreover it serves to distinguish from Werk (“work”).

noun:Wüterich.tx: Inherited from Middle High German wüeterī̌ch, wuoterī̌ch, from Old High German wuotarīh. By surface analysis, Wut + -rich.

noun:Wasserscheu.tx: Wasser + Scheu. Calque of Ancient Greek ὑδροφοβίᾱ (hudrophobíā).

noun:Wicke.tx: From Middle High German wicke, from Old High German wicka, from Proto-West Germanic *wikkjā. The sense of a worthless item derives from the opposition to cereal plants; now “Wicke” is rather praised as an ornamental plant. The idiom “in die Wicken gehen”, not to be tracked further than the nineteenth century and still rather rare, is less common with this noun than with Binsen and derives either …

noun:Wergeld.tx: From Middle High German wergelt, from Old High German werigelt, from Proto-West Germanic *werageld (literally “man-money”).

noun:Wasserklosett.tx: Wasser + Klosett, calque of English water closet.

noun:Wasserweg.tx: From Middle High German wazzerwec, from Old High German *wazzarweg, equivalent to Wasser + Weg. Cognate with Middle Low German wāterwech (“waterway”).

noun:Wasserlauf.tx: From Middle High German waȥȥerlouf. By surface analysis, Wasser + Lauf.

verb:wahrhaben.tx: Univerbation from an original colloquial set phrase wahr haben wollen.

noun:Wohltat.tx: From Middle High German woltāt, from Old High German wolatāt, woletāt, from Proto-Germanic *weladēdiz. By surface analysis, Wohl + Tat.

noun:Wickeltisch.tx: wickeln (“put a diaper/nappy [on a baby]”) + Tisch (“table”)

verb:wegtragen.tx: weg- + tragen. Compare English draw away.

noun:Wolfsmilch.tx: From Middle High German wolfsmilch, from Old High German wolfesmilch, *wolfesmiluh. Equivalent to Wolf (“wolf”) + -s- + Milch (“milk”), after the plant's acrid sap. Compare Dutch wolfsmelk and Polish wilczomlecz.

adj:wohlschmeckend.tx: wohl (“well”) + schmeckend (“tasting”). Compare Danish velsmagende, Swedish välsmakande.

adj:Wormser.tx: Worms + -er (forms invariable adjectives from place names)

noun:Wickel.tx: From Middle High German wickel, wickelin, from Old High German wickilī, wickilīn, diminutive of Old High German wiohha, from Proto-West Germanic *weukā (“flax bundle, wick”), from Proto-Indo-European *weg- (“to weave”).

adj:witzlos.tx: From Middle High German witzelōs, from Old High German wizzilos (“witless”). By surface analysis, Witz (“wit”) + -los (“-less”).

noun:Weltraumoper.tx: From Weltraum + Oper, calque of English space opera.

phrase:wenn's kein Schneider ist.tx: Literally, “if it’s not a tailor”. Origin unknown. The most plausible theory says that the original form was *wenn’s nicht der Schnitter ist (“if it’s not the [Grim] Reaper”). Then altered, either humorously or by taboo avoidance.

phrase:wo sich Fuchs und Hase gute Nacht.tx: Literally, “where the fox and the hare bid each other goodnight”.

noun:Weltbürger.tx: Welt (“world”) + Bürger (“citizen”), calque of Ancient Greek κοσμοπολίτης (kosmopolítēs).

noun:Wetterfrosch.tx: From Wetter (“weather”) + Frosch (“frog”). Some frogs climb up vegetation in warm weather, so it was erroneously believed that the same behaviour could also predict warmth.

noun:Worst-Case-Szenario.tx: Partial calque of English worst-case scenario.

verb:wertschätzen.tx: Univerbation of wert (“worth”) + schätzen (“to consider, appreciate”).

noun:Wecke.tx: From Middle High German wecke, from Old High German wecki, weggi (“wedge”), from Proto-Germanic *wagjaz. Cognate with Dutch wig (“wedge”), English wedge.

noun:Wurmfortsatz.tx: Calque of New Latin processus vermiformis.

noun:Weltliteratur.tx: Welt + Literatur, attributed to Johann Wolfgang von Goethe.

noun:Wappenspruch.tx: From Wappen (“coat of arms”) + Spruch (“motto, slogan”).

verb:wabern.tx: Middle High German waberen, cognate to English waver and wave.

phrase:wenn es nicht wahr ist, dann ist.tx: Calque of Italian se non è vero, è ben trovato (“if it isn't true, it's well invented”).

noun:Wiesn.tx: From Bavarian Wiesn, cognate to German Wiese.

noun:Windspiel.tx: Wind (“wind”) + spielen (“to play”), literally “something the wind is playing with”

verb:wuppen.tx: Variant of wippen, and like this a Central and Low German word. In some Low German dialects, wuppen is the regular outcome of Middle Low German wippen (cf. the development in Wucht). In other dialects, the same form was probably derived by playful neo-ablaut.

noun:Wartburg.tx: From Middle High German Wartberc and Burg. By surface analysis, Warte + Burg.

adv:weiters.tx: Adverbial strong genitive of weiter (“further”, comparative of weit).

noun:Wigwam.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English wigwam, from Abenaki wigwôm (“house”) or Penobscot wigwom (“house”), ultimately from Proto-Algonquian *wi·kiwa·ʔmi (“house”).

noun:Wieß.tx: From Central Franconian (Ripuarian) wieß (“white”), from wieß Bier (“white beer”). Compare Weißbier n, Weiße f (as in Berliner Weiße).

phrase:wenn das der Führer wüsste.tx: Literally, “if the Fuhrer knew of that!” The phrase is mostly associated with the belief, held by some Germans during the Third Reich, that Hitler did not condone violent excesses against Jews and other enemies of the regime, or even that he opposed some of the NSDAP's measures. However, it may have been used in other contexts as well. It may also have been chiefly sarcastic; compare English if only the tsar knew.

phrase:wir sind wieder wer.tx: Literally, “we are someone again”, that is, “we are respected again”.

noun:Windstille.tx: From Wind + Stille. Compare Dutch windstilte, Danish and Norwegian vindstille, Swedish vindstilla.

pt: to wander, move from place to place
noun:Wanderpokal.tx: From wandern (“to wander, move from place to place”) + Pokal (“cup, trophy”).

noun:Wasserschierling.tx: From Wasser + Schierling. Compare Dutch waterscheerling.

noun:Wunscherfüllung.tx: From Wunsch + Erfüllung. Probably coined by Sigmund Freud in 1899.

noun:Wechselschritt.tx: From Wechsel + Schritt or wechseln + Schritt.

phrase:was das Zeug hält.tx: Literally, “what[ever] the gear endures”. Likely referring to sails (Zeug meaning “fabric”), harnesses (cf. Zaumzeug), or the like.

verb:widersagen.tx: From Middle High German widersagen, from Old High German widarsagēn, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþrasaggjan. Equivalent to wider + sagen.

noun:Webpräsenz.tx: From web + Präsenz (presence), in the same vein as Internetpräsenz.

noun:Wendekreis.tx: From wenden + Kreis or Wende + Kreis.

noun:Wasserstraße.tx: From Middle High German waȥȥerstrāȥe. Equivalent to Wasser + Straße.

noun:Wegegeld.tx: From Middle High German wegegelt. Equivalent to Weg + -e- + Geld.

noun:Wohnadresse.tx: From wohnen (“to live, reside, dwell”) + Adresse (“address”).

noun:Wohnanschrift.tx: From wohnen (“to live, reside, dwell”) + Anschrift (“address”).

noun:Würfelspieler.tx: From Würfel (“dice”) + Spieler (“player”) or Würfelspiel (“game of dice”) + -er (“-er”).

phrase:wer lesen kann, ist klar im Vorte.tx: Literally, “those who can read have a clear advantage”. The earliest written attestation seems to be on Usenet in 1991 (see quotations), though spoken usage is likely older.

verb:widern.tx: From Middle High German wideren, widern, from Old High German widarōn. Equivalent to wider (“against”) + -n. Compare also zuwider with similar semantics.

adj:wohlgestaltet.tx: wohl + gestaltet, in place of the older and original wohlgestalt.

phrase:wie Sie sehen, sehen Sie nichts.tx: Literally, “as you can see, you can’t see anything”. First said by German TV host Hans-Joachim Kulenkampff when the lights went out during a live show.

noun:Waschtrockner.tx: Blend of Waschmaschine + Wäschetrockner. By surface analysis, waschen (“to wash”) + Trockner (“dryer”).

verb:wegkönnen.tx: weg- + können. Cognate with Bavarian wegkenna and Dutch wegkunnen.

noun:Wackes.tx: Uncertain. Usually assumed to be derived from wackeln (“to waggle”), or perhaps from Latin vagus (“wandering, rambling”), in either case, usually implying loitering or vagrancy.

adj:wohlgestalt.tx: Inherited from Middle High German wohlgestalt. By surface analysis, wohl + gestellt or wohl + Gestalt.

phrase:wie ein Affe auf dem Schleifstein.tx: Literally, “like a monkey on a whetstone”.

noun:Weißwasser.tx: From weiß (“white”) + Wasser (“water”). Most of the toponyms are calques from Slavic languages. The Lusatian town is attested as Middle High German Wyzzenwasser (14th c.), from Old Sorbian (cf. contemporary Upper Sorbian Běła Woda).

noun:Widerchrist.tx: From wider- + Christ, a calque of Latin antichrīstus.

noun:Wiederbewaffnung.tx: From wiederbewaffnen + -ung; equivalent to wieder (“again”) + -n- + Bewaffnung (“armament”).

phrase:wer nichts wird, wird Wirt.tx: Literally, “he who becomes nothing [in life], becomes an innkeeper”.

noun:Wärmeflasche.tx: From wärmen (“to warm”) + Flasche (“bottle”) or Wärme (“warmth”) + Flasche (“bottle”).

noun:Wunderbaum.tx: From Wunder (“wonder”) + Baum (“tree”). Sense 2 from a brand name.

noun:Wendigo.tx: Borrowed from Ojibwe wiindigoo, from Proto-Algonquian *wi·nteko·wa (“owl; malevolent spirit, cannibalistic monster”). Compare Plains Cree wîhtikow, ᐃᐧᐦᑎᑯᐤ (“greedy person; cannibal; giant man-eating monster”).

adj:wahnwitz.tx: Inherited from Middle High German wanwiz, wanwitze. Later displaced by wahnwitzig.
